# Education in Finland: Summary
Education in Finland is characterized by its comprehensive and egalitarian approach. All children have access to free universal daycare from eight months to five years, followed by a year of preschool at age six, which is not mandatory but almost universally used. The emphasis in early childhood education is on play, learning social skills, and developing "learning to learn" abilities rather than formal instruction. Formal schooling begins at age seven, with nine years of compulsory comprehensive basic education (grades 1–9). Since legislation in 2021, compulsory education includes either upper secondary academic schooling (lukio) or vocational school (ammatillinen koulutus), extending until age 18 unless older.
Schools are primarily funded and administered by municipalities; private schools exist but cannot charge tuition fees and must provide equivalent benefits and access as municipal schools. Class sizes are small, with teachers required to hold master’s degrees and admission to teaching programs highly competitive. The curriculum places value on autonomy for teachers, minimum homework, and equal opportunities for all students. Comprehensive school students receive free daily meals, books, materials, health care, and, if needed, housing.
After basic education, students may choose either academic upper secondary (with nationally graded matriculation examination necessary for university entry) or vocational training, both of which offer pathways to higher education. Tertiary education is split into research-focused universities and universities of applied sciences, with admissions determined by transparent, merit-based examinations. Tuition is free for Finnish and EU/EEA students; non-EU/EEA students pay fees. Adult education and lifelong learning are widely available, including Open University programs and "Free Education" institutes offering diverse personal development courses. The Finnish National Curriculum Framework (since 2016) mandates phenomenon-based learning and development of 21st-century skills throughout basic education.
Finland’s system is lauded for its equity, minimal standardized testing, multilingual instruction (students learn at least two foreign languages), and international education export programs.
